The 2026 US midterm elections have delivered a significant political setback to President Donald Trump, but their implications for US policy and global energy markets are far from straightforward. Democratic control of Congress will constrain the administration's domestic legislative agenda and yet leave considerable presidential discretion over foreign policy. The outcome closely matches Scenario C of our 5 October outlook: legislative gridlock at home, greater congressional influence over spending and appointments, and potentially increased reliance on executive powers to define the administration’s policies abroad. Rather than reversing the direction of US policy, the elections may change how it is pursued.

The US remains deeply involved in the Middle East conflict, energy prices remain elevated, and Washington increasingly uses sanctions, trade restrictions and energy resources as instruments of negotiation. A Democratic Congress could raise the political cost of further escalation against Iran, complicate potential concessions to Russia and increase scrutiny of trade policy. Yet, congressional constraints could also encourage greater reliance on executive action, potentially increasing rather than reducing geopolitical uncertainty. For energy markets, the most consequential effects may therefore emerge abroad, while domestic oil and gas production continues to respond primarily to market fundamentals.

Hence, there are important limits to what the election can change. The White House retains considerable authority over the instruments that impact global energy markets most directly: sanctions implementation, diplomacy and certain trade measures. Congress retains authority over trade legislation, appropriations and war powers, while the Supreme Court has already established legal limits on the use of emergency economic powers to levy tariffs. The election result would therefore put more political and institutional constraints on the administration's actions, rather than fundamentally altering the powers available to it.

Domestically, US oil and gas production will remain driven by market fundamentals, investment economics and infrastructure constraints. Critical-mineral supply chains, nuclear energy and geothermal retain scope for bipartisan cooperation. Data-center electricity demand adds a further dimension, with states, utilities and regulators holding substantial influence over investment and the allocation of infrastructure costs.

Timing now matters. The outgoing Congress retains its authority until the new one convenes on 3 January, and fiscal decisions taken in that window could constrain its successor. Subsequent budget and debt-limit negotiations will provide the first indication of how the new political balance translates into policy. The midterms will not resolve the strains from conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, or from transatlantic and US-Canada trade tensions. Still, they will change the political environment in which Washington responds to them. The central question for 2027 is whether these new constraints encourage accommodation, produce prolonged paralysis or drive the administration toward a more assertive use of executive power, with potentially significant consequences for global energy markets.

Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate. In the Senate, the party flipped seven seats, in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas, well beyond the net gain of four it needed, and now holds 54 seats to the Republicans' 44, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled. In the House, it is estimated Democrats will hold between 251 and 268 seats once all votes are counted, although dozens of races, 68 by the Associated Press's count on 4 November, had not yet been called.

Five of the seven flips came in states the Cook Political Report had rated toss-ups before the vote (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas). The other two, in North Carolina and South Carolina, fell outside that list. As of 6 November, two Senate races, in Alaska and Mississippi, remained uncalled. Neither can change control of the chamber.

Our outlook described a Democratic sweep producing legislative gridlock with some horse-trading on domestic energy policy. Each side's agenda stalls, but must-pass bills could force trades. In foreign policy, the scenario points to an executive workaround. Congress will seek to codify pressure on China and Russia and to add institutional brakes, while the White House could lean more on executive power to pursue its priorities abroad.

The president keeps his veto. Overriding one requires 67 senators and 290 House members, and the projected House majority – while larger than the narrow margin our analysis assumed – remains well short of that threshold. History points in the same direction. Over the last five presidencies, 81 of 84 vetoes came after the president's party lost a chamber. Congresses seated after such a flip enacted an average of 391 public laws, compared with 514 for all others.

The main new lever is control of money and people. Both chambers now control funding, and the Senate controls confirmations. On Iran, both chambers can pass war-powers resolutions, but the veto still holds, so the practical leverage lies in holding back war funding and confirmations. Our analysis concluded that Democratic gains make post-election escalation costlier and a deal likelier. On Russia, a Democratic Senate adds votes on Ukraine aid and the power to delay envoys and sanctions officials, which makes concessions pressed on Kyiv harder to sell.
